q: Who is the writer of Song of Songs?
a: Solomon is the writer of Song of Songs.

q: What does the young woman ask her lover to do?
a: The young woman asks her lover to kiss her with the kisses of his mouth.

q: What does the young woman say is better than wine?
a: The young woman says her lover’s love is better than wine.

q: What does the young woman say her lover’s name is like?
a: The young woman says his name is like fragrant oil.

q: Where has the king brought the young woman?
a: The king has brought the young woman into his rooms.

q: How does the young woman describe her skin?
a: The young woman describes her skin as dark but lovely like tents of Kedar, like curtains of Solomon.

q: Why does she not want the other women to stare at her?
a: She does not want the other women to stare at her because her skin is scorched.

q: What did the young woman’s brothers do when they were angry with her?
a: The young woman’s brothers made her a keeper of the vineyards.

q: What does the woman ask her lover?
a: She asks him where he feeds his flock and where he rests his flock at noontime.

q: How does her lover say the young woman can find him?
a: He tells her to follow the tracks of his flock to the shepherds’ tents.

q: To what does the young woman’s lover compare her?
a: He compares her to a mare among Pharaoh’s chariots.

q: What does her lover say is on her cheeks and neck?
a: He says earrings are on her cheeks and strings of jewels are on her neck.

q: What does her lover say he will make for her?
a: He says he will make for her gold earrings with silver studs.

q: Where was the king lying while the woman’s perfume spread in the room?
a: The king was lying on his couch while the fragrance of the woman’s perfume spread.

q: Where does her beloved spend the night?
a: Her beloved spends the night lying between her breasts.

q: To what does the young woman liken her beloved?
a: Her beloved is like a cluster of henna flowers in the vineyards of En Gedi.

q: How does her lover describe her eyes?
a: He says her eyes are like doves.

q: What does the woman say serves as their bed?
a: Leafy plants serve as their bed.

q: Of what does the woman say the beams and rafters of their house are made?
a: The beams and rafters are made of cedar and pine trees.

q: How does the woman describe herself?
a: She describes herself as a flower of the plain, a lily of the valleys.

q: What does the man say she was like among the daughters of his countrymen?
a: He said she was like a lily among thorns.

q: How does the woman describe her beloved among the young men?
a: The woman describes her young man as an apple tree among the trees of the forest.

q: Where did the woman sit?
a: She sat down under his shadow with great delight.

q: What was sweet to her taste?
a: His fruit was sweet to her taste.

q: Where did her young man bring her?
a: Her young man brought her to the house of wine.

q: What was his banner over her?
a: His banner over her was love.

q: What does the young woman want to sustain and refresh herself?
a: The young woman wants raisin cakes to sustain her and apples to refresh her.

q: Where is the young man’s left and right hands?
a: His left hand is under her head and his right hand embraces her.

q: What does the young woman want the daughters of Jerusalem to avoid?
a: The young woman wants the young women to avoid awakening love before the right time comes.

q: What sound does the young woman hear?
a: The young woman hears the voice of her beloved.

q: What does she say her beloved is doing?
a: He is leaping over the mountains and jumping over the hills.

q: What does she say her beloved is like?
a: She said her beloved is like a gazelle or a young stag.

q: What did her beloved want her to do with him?
a: He wanted her to get up and come with him.

q: What did he say was past, and what was over and gone?
a: He said the winter was gone and the rain had passed.

q: What has appeared in the land?
a: Flower blossoms have appeared in the land.

q: For what is it time?
a: It is time for song.

q: What ripens and what is in blossom?
a: The green fig tree ripens and the vines blossom.

q: What does her beloved want his beautiful one to do?
a: He wants her to arise and come with him.

q: What does her beloved call her?
a: Her beloved calls her his dove.

q: What does her beloved want to see and hear?
a: Her beloved wants to see her lovely appearance and hear her sweet voice.

q: What does the woman want him to catch?
a: The woman wants him to catch the little foxes that ruin vineyards.

q: To whom does the woman’s beloved belong?
a: Her beloved belongs to her.

q: To whom does the woman belong?
a: She belongs to her beloved.

q: What does her beloved do among the lilies?
a: He grazes among the lilies with pleasure.

q: What does she want her beloved to do?
a: She wants her beloved to turn to her.

q: When does she want her beloved to turn?
a: She wants her beloved to turn to her until the soft winds of dawn blow and the shadows flee away.

q: What does she want him to be like?
a: She wants him to be like a gazelle or a young stag on the rugged mountains.

q: For whom was the woman longing but could not find?
a: The woman was longing for the one whom she loved, but she could not find him.

q: For whom did the woman search through the streets and squares but not find?
a: The woman searched through the streets and squares, but she could not find her beloved.

q: What did the woman ask the watchmen when they found her?
a: She asked them, “Have you seen my beloved?”

q: When did she find the one whom her soul loved?
a: She found the one whom her soul loved just after she passed the watchmen in the city.

q: What did she do with her beloved?
a: She held him and would not let him go until she had brought him into her mother’s house.

q: What does the woman want the daughters of Jerusalem to promise?
a: The woman wants the daughters of Jerusalem to promise they would not awaken or stir love before the right time.

q: What does the young woman see coming from the wilderness that is perfumed with myrrh and frankincense and powders?
a: She sees the portable litter of Solomon coming with 60 warriors around it.

q: At what were the warriors good?
a: The warriors were good with the sword and in warfare.

q: What did King Solomon make for himself?
a: King Solomon made a sedan chair from wood from Lebanon.

q: What did King Solomon’s sedan chair look like?
a: The chair had posts of silver, a back of gold, a seat of purple cloth, and was decorated and made comfortable with love from the daughters of Jerusalem.

q: At what does the young woman want the women of Jerusalem to look?
a: She wants them to look at King Solomon.

q: What was King Solomon wearing on his marriage day?
a: He wore a crown with which his mother crowned him on his marriage day.

q: How does the woman’s lover describe her eyes?
a: Her eyes are as doves behind her veil.

q: How does the woman’s lover describe her hair?
a: Her hair is like a flock of goats hopping down Mount Gilead.

q: How does her lover describe her teeth?
a: Her teeth are like a flock of newly shorn and washed sheep, two of each and none missing.

q: What does the woman’s beloved say about her lips and mouth?
a: He says that her lips are like a thread of scarlet and that her mouth is lovely.

q: How does the woman’s beloved describe her cheeks?
a: He describes her cheeks as being like pomegranate halves behind her veil.

q: How does the woman’s beloved describe her neck?
a: He describes her neck as the tower of David built in rows of stone with a thousand soldiers’ shields hanging on it.

q: How does the woman’s beloved describe her two breasts?
a: He describes her two breasts as two fawns, twins of a gazelle, grazing among the lilies.

q: Where will her lover go until dawn comes and the shadows flee?
a: He says he will go to the mountain of myrrh and the hill of frankincense.

q: In what way is his love beautiful?
a: She is beautiful in every way.

q: What does his beautiful love not have?
a: His beautiful love does not have any blemish.

q: What does Solomon call his bride?
a: Solomon calls her his sister.

q: What does Solomon say the love of his wife is better than?
a: Solomon says her love is better than wine.

q: What is the smell of her perfume better than?
a: The smell of her perfume is better than any spice.

q: With what does he say his bride’s lips drip, and what is under her tongue?
a: He says his bride’s lips drip with nectar, and she has honey and milk under her tongue.

q: What does the woman’s clothes smell like?
a: Her clothes smell like the fragrance of Lebanon.

q: What kind of garden and what kind of spring does Solomon say his sister, his bride, is like?
a: Solomon says she is like a garden locked up and a spring that is sealed.

q: To what does he liken the woman’s shoots?
a: He likens her shoots to a grove of pomegranate trees with choice fruit and plants and all the finest spices.

q: With what kinds of water does Solomon describe his lover?
a: He describes her as a garden spring, a well of fresh water, and streams flowing down from Lebanon.

q: On what does the young woman want the north and south winds to blow and why?
a: She wants the north and south winds to blow on her garden so that its spices would give off their fragrance.

q: What does she want her beloved to do and to eat?
a: She wants her beloved to come into his garden and to eat some of its choice fruit.

q: Where has Solomon come?
a: Solomon has come into his garden.

q: Of what is Solomon’s bride dreaming?
a: She is dreaming of her beloved’s knocking and talking.

q: What has Solomon’s beloved already done?
a: She has already taken off her robe and washed her feet.

q: Where had Solomon put his hand?
a: Solomon had put his hand through the opening of the door latch.

q: With what were the bride’s hands dripping when she opened the door?
a: Her hands were dripping with moist myrrh.

q: What did the bride find when she opened the door and how did she feel?
a: She found that her beloved had turned and gone, so her heart sank and she became sad.

q: What did the watchmen do when they found Solomon’s bride?
a: They struck and wounded her and took away her veil.

q: What does the bride ask the women of Jerusalem to promise?
a: She asks the women of Jerusalem to promise that if they find her beloved they will tell him she is lovesick for him.

q: How does the young woman’s beloved make her feel?
a: The young woman’s beloved makes her feel sick with love.

q: What do the young women ask of the bride?
a: They ask her how and why her beloved is better than another beloved.

q: How does the young woman describe her beloved?
a: She describes him as radiant, ruddy, and outstanding.

q: How does the woman describe her beloved’s head and hair?
a: She describes his head as pure gold and his hair as curly and black.

q: How does the woman describe her beloved’s eyes?
a: She describes his eyes like doves washed in milk.

q: How does Solomon’s bride describe his cheeks and lips?
a: She describes his cheeks like spice gardens and his lips like myrrh-soaked lilies.

q: How does the woman describe her beloved’s arms and abdomen?
a: She describes his arms as rods of gold with topaz and his abdomen as a plate of ivory covered with sapphires.

q: How does the woman describe her beloved’s legs and his appearance?
a: She describes his legs as marble pillars with gold bases and his appearance like Lebanon, as special as the cedars.

q: How does Solomon’s bride describe her beloved’s mouth and Solomon himself to Jerusalem’s daughters?
a: She describes his mouth as most sweet and that Solomon is most desirable.

q: What questions do the women of Jerusalem ask of the young woman?
a: They ask her where her beloved has gone and whether they can go with her to look for him.

q: For what did the young women want to seek?
a: The young women wanted to seek for the young woman’s beloved.

q: What does the young woman say her beloved was doing?
a: The young woman said he was in his spice gardens to graze in the garden and to gather lilies.

q: To whom do the young woman and her lover belong?
a: The young woman and her lover belong to each other.

q: Where does the young woman’s lover graze?
a: The young woman’s lover grazes among the lilies.

q: What two cities does the woman’s lover use to describe her?
a: He describes her as two cities, Tirzah and Jerusalem.

q: How does her beloved feel about her?
a: He feels that she is completely beautiful and lovely, but also awe-inspiring.

q: Why does the woman’s lover want her to turn her eyes away from him?
a: The woman’s lover wants her to turn her eyes away from him because her eyes excite him.

q: How does the woman’s lover describe her hair?
a: He describes her hair as a flock of goats descending the slopes of Mount Gilead.

q: How does her lover describe her teeth?
a: He describes her teeth as a flock of ewes, each with twins and none missing, coming up from the washing place.

q: How does her lover describe her cheeks?
a: Her lover describes her cheeks as pomegranate halves behind her veil.

q: How many other women does the woman’s lover say there may be?
a: He says there may be 60 queens, 80 concubines, and young women without number.

q: How does the woman’s lover describe his dove?
a: The woman’s lover describes her as pure, the only one, and the special and favorite daughter of her mother.

q: What did the queens and the concubines say about her when they saw her?
a: The queens and concubines called her blessed, and they praised her.

q: How does the woman’s lover describe her?
a: The woman’s lover describes her like the dawn, the moon, the sun, and as completely awesome.

q: Why did the woman’s lover go into the grove of nut trees?
a: The woman’s lover went into the grove of nut trees to see if the vines had budded and the pomegranates were in bloom.

q: How did the woman’s lover feel?
a: The woman’s lover felt as though he were riding in the chariot of a prince.

q: What did the woman’s lover want her to do?
a: The woman’s lover wanted her to turn back to him.

q: Why does the woman’s lover want her to turn to him?
a: The woman’s lover wants her to turn to him so that he might gaze on her.

q: What does the man ask the other people?
a: He asks why they look at her as if mesmerized by a dancer.

q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s feet in her sandals and the curves of her thighs?
a: He describes her feet in her sandals as beautiful and the curves of her thighs like the work of a craftsman.

q: How does Solomon describe his love’s navel and belly?
a: Solomon describes his love’s navel as a round bowl which never lacks spiced wine and her belly as a mound of wheat surrounded with lilies.

q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s two breasts?
a: Solomon describes her two breasts like two fawns, twins of a gazelle.

q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s neck, eyes, and nose?
a: Solomon describes her neck as an ivory tower, her eyes like a pool, and her nose like the tower of Lebanon.

q: How does Solomon describe his lover’s head and hair?
a: Solomon describes her head like Mount Carmel and her hair like purple, captivating him.

q: How does Solomon describe his lover and her breasts?
a: He describes her height as a date palm tree and her breasts as date clusters.

q: What does he also want his lover’s breasts and breath to be like?
a: He also wants his lover’s breasts to be like date clusters and her breath to be sweet like dates and the smell of an apple.

q: What does he want his lover’s mouth to be like?
a: He wants her mouth to be like the best wine.

q: To whom does the young woman belong and whom does he desire?
a: The young woman belongs to her beloved, and her beloved desires her.

q: Where does the young woman want her beloved to go with her?
a: She wants him to go into the countryside to spend the night in the villages.

q: Why does she want her beloved to rise early?
a: She wants him to rise early to see if the vines in the vineyards have budded and if the pomegranates have begun blooming.

q: What does she say she will give to her beloved when they get to the vineyards?
a: She says she will give him her love.

q: What does she say the mandrakes would do?
a: She says the mandrakes would give off their fragrance.

q: What does she say was at the door where she and her lover were staying?
a: She says that at the door where they were staying there were all sorts of choice fruits, new and old, that she had stored up for him.

q: What does the woman wish that her lover was like and why?
a: She wishes he were like her brother so that she could kiss her lover at any time and no one would despise her.

q: Where would the woman have liked to bring her lover?
a: She would have liked to bring him to her mother’s house.

q: What were her lover’s left and right hands doing?
a: His left hand was holding her head and his right hand was embracing her.

q: What does the woman want Jerusalem’s women to promise?
a: The woman wants Jerusalem’s women to promise that they would not stir up love before its proper time.

q: What do the women of Jerusalem ask?
a: They ask who is coming up from the wilderness, leaning on her beloved.

q: What did the young woman tell her lover when she woke him under the apple tree?
a: She told him that his mother had conceived and given birth to him under the apple tree.

q: What does the young woman want her lover to do and why?
a: She wants him to set her as a seal over his heart, because love is as strong as death, and jealousy flashes like a hot flame.

q: What could not stop love?
a: Floods of water could not put out the fire of love.

q: What does the woman’s brothers say about their little sister?
a: They said that her breasts had not yet grown and that they wondered what they would do for her when she is promised in marriage.

q: What would the woman’s brothers do if she were a wall?
a: If she were a wall, they would build a tower of silver on her.

q: What would the woman’s brothers do if she were a door?
a: If she were a door, they would cover her with boards of cedar.

q: How did the young woman describe herself?
a: She described herself as a wall with breasts large like towers, and completely mature.

q: What did the young woman say that Solomon did with his vineyard at Baal Hamon?
a: Solomon leased his vineyard to those who would take care of it.

q: What does the young woman say about her own vineyard and those who maintained it?
a: She said the 1000 shekels that it brought belonged to Solomon and that those who maintained it would get 200 shekels.

q: What did the woman’s lover say to her who lived in the gardens, about what his friends, as well as he, wanted to hear?
a: He said that his friends, as well as he, wanted to be the ones to hear her voice.

q: What does the young woman want her beloved to do and to be like?
a: She wants her beloved to hurry and to be like a deer.
